elements.quote: Our living systematic review (LSR) focuses on suicide prevention in relation to COVID-19
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a (living) systematic review.

elements.quote: Our living systematic review (LSR) focuses on suicide prevention in relation to COVID-19
elements.reason: The abstract provides an explicit statement of the main objective/focus of the review.

elements.quote: Eligibility criteria include incidence/prevalence of suicidal behaviour, exposure-outcome relationships and effects of interventions in relation to the COVID-19 pandemic. Outcomes of interest are suicide, self-harm or attempted suicide and suicidal thoughts. No restrictions are placed on language or study type, except for single-person case reports.
elements.reason: Main inclusion criteria are described (e.g., incidence/prevalence, outcomes of interest), but the abstract does not clearly specify main inclusion and exclusion criteria as separate comprehensive sets; it only notes one exclusion exception (single-person case reports).
The abstract does not identify the information sources used to identify studies/reports or when each source was last searched.
The abstract does not specify methods used to assess risk of bias in included studies.
The abstract describes automation and eligibility but does not specify methods used to present and synthesize the results (e.g., how findings were synthesized).

elements.quote: Searches identified 2070 articles, 29 (28 studies) met our inclusion criteria
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies and (by implication from inclusion) included articles.

elements.quote: No studies reported on changes in rates of suicidal behaviour.
elements.reason: The abstract provides results for at least one main outcome-related finding (no studies reported changes in rates), but it does not clearly present results for each main outcome including the number of included studies and participants per outcome.

elements.quote: No studies reported on changes in rates of suicidal behaviour.
elements.reason: The abstract reports no studies on the main rate-change outcome and does not indicate that a meta-analysis was conducted.

elements.quote: Our living systematic review (LSR) focuses on suicide prevention in relation to COVID-19, with this iteration synthesising relevant evidence up to June 7 th 2020.
elements.reason: The abstract does not describe comparisons between groups (direction of effect and which group is favored is not reported).

elements.quote: However, suicide data are challenging to collect in real time and economic effects are evolving.
elements.reason: The abstract includes limitations/challenges relevant to the included evidence (difficulty collecting suicide data in real time and evolving economic effects).

elements.quote: There is thus far no clear evidence of an increase in suicide, self-harm, suicidal behaviour, or suicidal thoughts associated with the pandemic.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding for the review.
The abstract does not provide the register name and registration number.

elements.quote:
“Given the health and economic threats posed by the pandemic to the global community, there are concerns that rates of suicide and suicidal behaviour may rise during and in its aftermath.”

“…there is thus far no clear evidence of an increase in suicide, self-harm, suicidal behaviour, or suicidal thoughts associated with the pandemic. However, suicide data are challenging to collect in real time and economic effects are evolving.”
elements.reason: Describes existing concerns and indicates an important uncertainty (“thus far no clear evidence…”) and some limitations/challenges (“suicide data are challenging to collect in real time”). However, it does not clearly describe the broader current state of knowledge and uncertainties in a comprehensive way beyond this framing.

elements.quote: “Our living systematic review (LSR) focuses on suicide prevention in relation to COVID-19… Our LSR will provide a regular synthesis of the most up-to-date research evidence to guide public health and clinical policy to mitigate the impact of COVID-19 on suicide.”
elements.reason: Explains why the review is needed by stating it will synthesize up-to-date evidence to guide public health and clinical policy.
No evidence was provided that the manuscript explains the need for the review in light of similar systematic reviews, including updates/replications and citations of previous reviews.

The conditional requirement refers to reviews of intervention effects and the mechanism of action of an intervention. The retrieved evidence describes a living systematic review focused on evidence related to COVID-19 exposure/outcomes and synthesis, but does not provide intervention mechanism information indicating an intervention-effect review.

The conditional requirement is for complex interventions or delivery contexts and would require a logic model. The retrieved evidence does not indicate a logic model is used or needed for the review’s scope based on the provided excerpts.

elements.quote: The overarching aim of the review is to identify and appraise any newly published evidence from around the world that assesses the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on suicide deaths, suicidal behaviours, self-harm and suicidal thoughts, or that assesses the effectiveness of strategies to reduce the risk of suicide deaths, suicidal behaviours, self-harm and suicidal thoughts, resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic.
elements.reason: The review’s overall aim is explicitly stated, but the evidence provided does not show that the objectives/questions are explicitly formulated using a specific relevant question-formulation framework (beyond describing outcomes/assessments).
No evidence was provided stating planned comparisons for intervention effects (e.g., PICO or appropriate variant).

elements.quote: Study participants may be adults or children of any ethnicities living in any country. Outcomes of interest are:  Deaths by suicide  Self-harm (intentional self-injury or self-poisoning regardless of motivation and intent) or attempted suicide (including hospital attendance and/or admission for these reasons)  Suicidal thoughts/ideation Figure 1. Workflow for updating the living systematic review review. The process will be supported using automation technology and at three-monthly intervals the team will update the published version of the review.
elements.reason: The evidence specifies participant characteristics and the outcomes of interest, but it does not fully specify all study-characteristic components needed for eligibility (e.g., eligible study designs, settings, and follow-up requirements) in a complete, checklist-like way.

elements.quote: Eligibility criteria include incidence/prevalence of suicidal behaviour, exposure-outcome relationships and effects of interventions in relation to the COVID-19 pandemic. Outcomes of interest are suicide, self-harm or attempted suicide and suicidal thoughts. No restrictions are placed on language or study type, except for single-person case reports.
elements.reason: The evidence states there are no language restrictions and an exception for single-person case reports, but it does not clearly specify eligibility criteria for report characteristics such as dissemination year and publication/report status.
No evidence was retrieved that distinguishes exclusions where outcomes were not measured versus exclusions where outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: We synthesised studies according to themes based on research questions and study design, using tables and narrative. Results were synthesised separately for studies in the general population, in health and social care staff and other at-risk occupations, and in vulnerable populations (e.g. people of older age or those with underlying conditions that predispose them to becoming severely ill or dying after contracting COVID-19).
elements.reason: The evidence specifies groups used for synthesis (general population; health/social care staff/other at-risk occupations; vulnerable populations) and indicates they are based on research questions and study design, but it does not explicitly link these groups to specific comparisons defined in the review objectives.
Although a notable restriction is mentioned (exclusion of single-person case reports), no rationale for this or other eligibility restrictions is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: A sample search strategy (for PubMed) appears in Box 1 from 1 st Jan 2020 to June 7 th 2020. ... For this version of the living review, Psy- and SocArXiv searches were carried out retrospectively on the 12 th of June, using a publication date filter for Jan 1 st 2020 - June 7 th 2020.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports a last-search date range/cutoff for (at least) PubMed (Jan 1 2020 to June 7 2020) and specifies that PsyArXiv/SocArXiv were carried out on 12 June; however, it does not clearly provide the last searched/consulted date for each listed information source (e.g., PubMed, Scopus, CORD-19, WHO database) individually.

elements.quote: We searched the following electronic databases: PubMed; Scopus; medRxiv, bioRxiv; the COVID-19 Open Research Dataset (CORD-19) by Semantic Scholar and the Allen Institute for AI, which includes relevant records from Microsoft Academic, Elsevier, arXiv and PMC; and the WHO COVID-19 database. A sample search strategy (for PubMed) appears in Box 1 from 1 st Jan 2020 to June 7 th 2020.
elements.reason: Database names are provided, but the search interface/platform and available coverage dates are not reported for each database individually (only a sample strategy date range is given for PubMed, and coverage dates for other databases are not explicitly specified).
No study registers/regulatory databases/online repositories searched (as distinct from electronic databases and preprint repositories) are explicitly described in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved evidence does not report searching specific websites/search engines/online sources with names and URLs as separate from the listed electronic databases and repositories.
The retrieved evidence does not mention any organisations or manufacturers contacted to identify studies.
The retrieved evidence does not describe types of individuals contacted to identify studies.
The retrieved evidence does not specify the types of reference lists examined.
The retrieved evidence does not describe backward/forward citation searching (seed reports, citation index/platform, or search date).
The retrieved evidence does not report any journals or conference proceedings consulted, including source names, dates covered, or search methods.

elements.quote: A sample search strategy (for PubMed) appears in Box 1 from 1 st Jan 2020 to June 7 th 2020.
elements.reason: Only a sample PubMed search strategy is provided; the full search strategies as actually run are not reported for all databases/registers/websites (e.g., Scopus, bioRxiv/medRxiv, CORD-19, WHO database, PsyArXiv/SocArXiv).

elements.quote: No restrictions were placed on the types of study design eligible for inclusion, except for the exclusion of single-person case reports. There was no restriction on language of publication. We will draw on a combination of internet-based translation systems and network of colleagues to translate evidence in a language other than English. For this version of the living review, Psy- and SocArXiv searches were carried out retrospectively on the 12 th of June, using a publication date filter for Jan 1 st 2020 - June 7 th 2020.
elements.reason: Some limits are described (e.g., exclusion of single-person case reports; no language restriction; and a publication date filter for PsyArXiv/SocArXiv). However, the evidence does not show that all limits used across all sources are described and justified by reference to the eligibility criteria.
No explicit citation of published search approaches/filters is shown for use in the search strategies, nor descriptions of adaptations to such filters.
No natural-language processing or text-analysis tools are reported for identifying or refining search terms.
While translation systems are mentioned to translate evidence, the evidence does not specify tools used to translate search strings between sources.
No validation of the search strategy (process or validation studies) is described.
No peer review of the search strategy is described (e.g., no mention of PRESS or related process).
There is no description of a final conceptual structure and explorations for developing it when the search structure was not based on PICO.

elements.quote: A two-stage screening process was undertaken to identify studies meeting the eligibility criteria. First, two authors (either CO or EE) assessed citations from the searches and identified potentially relevant titles and abstracts. Second, either DG, AJ or RW assessed the full texts of potentially eligible studies to identify studies to be included in the review.
elements.reason: Reports the number of reviewers at each screening stage (two authors for citations/titles/abstracts; one of DG/AJ/RW for full texts).
The evidence describes who assessed each stage, but does not state whether reviewers worked independently at each screening stage.

elements.quote: Disagreements were resolved through discussion, and where this failed, by referral to a third reviewer (KH, NK or PM).
elements.reason: Explicitly describes how disagreements were resolved (discussion, then referral to a third reviewer).
No process is described for obtaining or confirming eligibility information from study investigators.

elements.quote: We will draw on a combination of internet-based translation systems and network of colleagues to translate evidence in a language other than English.
elements.reason: Describes methods for translating non-English evidence for eligibility assessment.

elements.quote: We have developed a workflow that automates daily searches of these databases, and the code supporting this process can be found at https://github. com/mcguinlu/COVID_suicide_living. Searches are conducted daily via PubMed and Scopus application programme interface and the bioRxiv and medRxiv RSS feeds.
elements.reason: Indicates automation technology is used within the review workflow (automated daily searches via APIs/RSS feeds).

elements.quote: One author (DG, AJ or RW) extracted data from each included study using a piloted data extraction form (see extended data (John & Schmidt, 2020)), and the extracted data were checked by one other author (AJ, or EE where AJ extracted data).
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the number of reviewers involved in data extraction from each included report/study (one extractor, checked by one other author).

elements.quote: One author (DG, AJ or RW) extracted data from each included study using a piloted data extraction form (see extended data (John & Schmidt, 2020)), and the extracted data were checked by one other author (AJ, or EE where AJ extracted data).

elements.quote: Data synthesis We synthesised studies according to themes based on research questions and study design, using tables and narrative. Results were synthesised separately for studies in the general population, in health and social care staff and other at-risk occupations, and in vulnerable populations (e.g. people of older age or those with underlying conditions that predispose them to becoming severely ill or dying after contracting COVID-19). The current document is the first iteration of our review. We have not considered it appropriate to combine any results identified so far in a meta-analysis.

elements.quote: To date, there is little literature exploring COVID-19 and suicide deaths, suicidal behaviours, self-harm and suicidal thoughts and most of the published evidence that we identified had important limitations. Importantly, much of the literature is not yet peer reviewed so the quality of reported studies may change. There were eight research letters, five pre-prints and for many others very short timeframes between submission and acceptance. All included studies were observational in design and prone to multiple sources of bias (eg, recall bias, selection bias, confounding). No conclusions can be drawn regarding causality and temporality from cross sectional studies. However, such study designs may be appropriate in current circumstances where timeliness of studies to inform policy and practice are important. However many were carried out too quickly and too early (one to two weeks post lockdown) in the outbreak to make meaningful contributions to the evidence base. The lack of baseline data in the majority of surveys included in the review and adjustments made to standardised measures to assess suicidal behaviours as well as the range of measures and timing asked made assessment of findings problematic.
elements.reason: The evidence explicitly discusses limitations of the studies included in the review (e.g., lack of peer review, observational design with bias, inability to infer causality/temporality, short timeframes, lack of baseline data, and problematic measurement/adjustments).
